clinicalPearls: A chronic neutrophilic scarring alopecia forming part of the follicular occlusion tetrad together with hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata and pilonidal sinus
Presents with tender, boggy, fluctuant nodules and interconnecting sinuses on the vertex and occiput that discharge pus and cause patchy scarring alopecia
Pressure on one nodule may express pus from a distant opening, reflecting the interconnecting subcutaneous tracts
It predominantly affects young adult men, especially those of African descent
Follicular occlusion with secondary bacterial colonisation drives the deep suppurative inflammation, so it is not a primary infection
Advanced disease produces hypertrophic scarring, keloids and permanent hair loss with loss of follicular ostia
Management is difficult and includes anti-inflammatory antibiotic-class therapy, drainage of abscesses, and oral retinoid or biologic therapy in refractory disease, with surgery for scarred sinuses
reference.pathophysiology: Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp begins with follicular hyperkeratosis and occlusion, leading to follicular rupture, deep dermal and subcutaneous neutrophilic inflammation, abscess formation and interconnecting sinus tracts. Secondary bacterial colonisation amplifies the suppuration. As a component of the follicular occlusion tetrad it shares this pathogenic mechanism with hidradenitis suppurativa and acne conglobata. Chronic inflammation and sinus formation destroy follicles and produce extensive fibrosis with permanent, scarring alopecia.
additionalDifferentials: Folliculitis decalvans, with pustules and tufting but less bogginess
Kerion, a fungal infection with positive mycology
Other nodular scalp conditions such as cutis verticis gyrata
additionalInvestigations: Bacterial swab and culture to guide antibacterial therapy and exclude a primary infection
Trichoscopy and clinical assessment of sinus interconnection
Scalp biopsy showing deep neutrophilic and granulomatous inflammation with sinus tracts
Screening for associated follicular occlusion tetrad conditions such as hidradenitis suppurativa and pilonidal sinus
redFlags: Extensive interconnecting sinuses with progressive scarring and keloid formation
Signs of deep or systemic infection
Long-standing disease with new indurated or non-healing areas, given the rare risk of squamous carcinoma
Severe refractory disease affecting quality of life, prompting escalation to systemic therapy
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic and relapsing with a tendency to permanent scarring alopecia and keloids; response to treatment is variable and often incomplete, and refractory disease may require systemic retinoids, biologics or surgery.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent nodules as isolated abscesses rather than recognising the interconnected disease
Missing the association with hidradenitis suppurativa and other occlusion-tetrad conditions
Under-treating with short antibiotic courses, allowing progression to scarring
Overlooking the small long-term risk of malignant change in chronic sinuses
management: Oral retinoids such as isotretinoin are the mainstay to reduce follicular occlusion and suppurative inflammation
Give antibacterials such as tetracyclines guided by swab culture for secondary bacterial colonisation
Use biologic therapy with a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab for refractory disease, reflecting the shared pathogenesis with hidradenitis suppurativa
Provide symptom relief with intralesional corticosteroids and incision and drainage of fluctuant abscesses
Add adjuncts such as oral zinc and antiseptic and keratolytic scalp care
Reserve surgical excision of extensive sinus tracts or laser epilation for recalcitrant disease
Screen for and manage associated follicular occlusion tetrad conditions including hidradenitis suppurativa and pilonidal sinus
Maintain dermatology follow-up given the chronic relapsing scarring course
